speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRESS RELEASE ISSUED BY U.S. DEPARTMENT OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday at 6.15 p.m. the department of state of the United States issued a statement to the press, in both Ottawa and Washington, on which I should like to comment.
That release was communicated to our ambassador in Washington and to our Department of External Affairs in Ottawa one half hour before it was handed to the press.

subtopic: PRESS RELEASE ISSUED BY U.S. DEPARTMENT OF STATE
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRESS RELEASE ISSUED BY U.S. DEPARTMENT OF STATE
speechtext:
I find it difficult to
understand such an extraordinary procedure. I want to speak, as always, on matters affecting a great neighbour and friendly nations with restraint, but also with responsibility. Quite apart from the terms of the statement, this action by the department of state of the United States is unprecedented, and I weigh my words when I say that it constitutes an unwarranted intrusion in Canadian affairs.
Mr. Speaker, in the statement the views of the department of state are expressed as to what it considers measures which Canada ought to take in relation to NATO and NORAD defences. These are surely matters for decision by Canada. As I read the document which was issued, it bears a striking resemblance to the statements made here last Friday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
On Friday last I expressed the views of the Canadian government on these matters, and I am not going to enter into any argument regarding the questions of detail dealt therein, except to say that the government sees no need to modify the views then expressed. The government of Canada does not consider that open public pressures by way of press releases or otherwise are appropriate methods of exchanging views as between equal sovereign nations and allies. There are well recognized channels for the exchange of points of view between sovereign countries and allies even when these points of view differ, as they must; and I express my very
great regret that the United States department of state did not see fit to follow the usual course in communicating its views. We have asked the Canadian ambassador to Washington to return to Ottawa in order to give us his first hand views regarding this matter.
Having said that, I want to emphasize this. The Canadian government will continue to work and strive for understanding and cooperation. It will, as always, honour its obligations. But it will not be pushed around or accept external domination or interference in the making of its decisions. Canada is determined to remain a firm ally, but that does not mean that she should be a satellite.

That statement coming from the Prime Minister of this country, Mr. Speaker, is unworthy of him.

government considered it necessary to issue any such statement about the speech of the Prime Minister and about the public statement on national defence of the Minister of National Defence. Questions of Canadian policy should be left entirely for discussion and decision to Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
The Prime Minister and his party have no monopoly of the determination of any party to stand up for Canada's rights in these matters against anybody. I suggest, however, that the rule also applies to Canadian governments and should be observed by them.
Having said that, may I add that it is important to be absolutely clear about what is involved in this matter. The statement made by the government of the United States, as indeed in large part the statement made by the Prime Minister of Canada last Friday and the clarification statement made by the Minister of National Defence subsequently- all these concern, Mr. Speaker, joint arrangements of the two countries for our common defence, joint arrangements entered into by this government for Canada.
The real issue for Canadians is, what are the facts and what is the truth? What is the truth about our defence policy in this common effort on this matter? The Canadian people and their representatives in parliament are entitled to learn the facts and to know the truth. On Saturday and again on Monday the Minister of National Defence, in a public statement of clarification, contradicted certain of the Prime Minister's statements.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PRESS RELEASE ISSUED BY U.S. DEPARTMENT OF STATE

and allies. Let us also remember that the real threat to Canada's security does not come from the United States but from communist imperialism, and unnecessary disputes among the western allies will weaken us all. There are at the moment enough differences in the free world today without adding one between Canada and the United States.
So, Mr. Speaker, any political leader in either country who for political, partisan purposes stirs up or enlarges any difference between the two countries-

subtopic: PRESS RELEASE ISSUED BY U.S. DEPARTMENT OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have witnessed in the last few hours an unprecedented action by a friendly government, that of the United States of America, against this country, Canada, in a way that to me is blatant interference in Canadian affairs. As has already been stated publicly through the press, the action taken by the United States government is the most severe ever taken during peacetime toward Canada. It would seem to me that there could have been far more friendly and effective ways of expressing a statement which obviously, through our own indecision in Canada, we have goaded the United States into making.
We have been told that we are in conference with the United States concerning what should be the policy of our two governments concerning defensive nuclear armament. Surely this conference table could have been one means of expressing the thoughts of the United States government. Then there are the normal diplomatic channels. I am sure that I express the sentiments of the Canadian people from Newfoundland to Vancouver island when I say that we resent the action the United States has taken, not so much for what was said but for the way that government has seen fit to say it. I agree that the United States of America is our closest friend and our best customer. However, I agree also with our Prime Minister that we, as Canadians, will not be pushed around.

The Prime Minister has said he will not be pushed around in the making of decisions.
I ask him again, what are those decisions? This is not a question that has been asked only by those who are members in this House of Commons. This is a question that is being asked by Canadians across the country. This is a question that the members of the press are asking as well. I should like to quote from an editorial that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of last night.

Certainly we ought to have a sense of responsibility in this matter so that we can make clear something which is not very difficult, because I do not think any of us are too far apart on it. Then we would not be forcing the United States into making statements which define our policy for us.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is not the time for a debate in connection with this problem. I believe we would never have been in this particular situation if a little different action had been taken. Mr. Speaker, there are two parts of this statement which was issued yesterday to which I think the house ought to have its attention drawn. The first is this:
The provision of nuclear weapons to Canadian forces would not involve an expansion of independent nuclear capability, or an increase in the

External Affairs
"nuclear club". As in the case of other allies custody of U.S. nuclear weapons would remain with the U.S. joint control fully consistent with national sovereignty can be worked out to cover the use of such weapons by Canadian forces.
That is the end of the statement. I wish to point out first, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the view which the United States took when nuclear missiles, presumably under the control of the Soviet union, were stationed in Cuba. The United States quite properly took the position at that time that this was an extension of the nuclear club, and that it did alter the balance of nuclear power.
May I point out, second, that it is for the Canadian people, through their elected representatives, to decide whether or not the acquisition of nuclear arms will expand the nuclear club and increase the danger of nuclear war. We in this party contend that stopping the spread of nuclear arms is a prelude to securing a cessation of nuclear tests and to reaching a treaty on nuclear disarmament. This is a Canadian decision, which has to be taken by Canadians and any attempt by any outside government to dictate to Canadians what their policy should be regarding the acquisition of nuclear arms will be both resented and ignored.
The other sentence in this statement to which I should like to draw the attention of the house is this:
A flexible and balanced defence requires increased conventional forces, but conventional forces are not an alternative to effective NATO or NORAD defence arrangements using nuclear-capable weapons systems.
Our membership in NATO is not conditional upon our accepting nuclear weapons. That is shown by the fact that other members of the alliance have not accepted nuclear weapons. If the Canadian people want to decide, as we think they should decide, upon a non-nuclear role for Canada, that is a decision which they have a right to make without any advice or any attempted intimidation from outside.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent and public importance, namely the statement made last night by the United States department of state contradicting recent statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence concerning the joint defence arrangements of the Canadian and United States governments.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I will be interested to hear remarks about the urgency of debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I wish to make four points, Mr. Speaker, any one of which might be considered fatal to the motion to adjourn the regular business of the house as proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. First of all I think we should be setting a dangerous precedent for ourselves if we were

to allow every unfavourable press release by a foreign power to precipitate us into debate while we are running the affairs of our own country. It does not take much imagination to foresee that if we postpone our regular business at this time for such a reason, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, other countries might be quick to use this as a tool against us.
The second point I wish to make has to do with citation No. 100 to be found on page 90 of Beauchesne. Paragraph 3 of that citation states that urgency within rule 26 does not apply to the subject matter itself but means urgency of debate when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that a discussion take place immediately. I submit, without argument as to the urgency of this subject matter, that there is not the urgency of debate required within the framework of Beauchesne's interpretation of the rules and practice of the house.
The third point I wish to make again relates to Beauchesne, and the point is whether the public interest would suffer if this matter were not discussed at once. As Dr. Beauchesne has written in citation 100, paragraph 2:
The "definite matter of urgent public importance", for the discussion of which the adjournment of the house may be moved under standing order 26, must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
We have heard the statement from the Prime Minister that the Canadian ambassador will shortly be in Ottawa to report on this matter, and I submit it would be more in the public interest to defer debate until the government had received the benefit of such briefing.
The fourth and final point I wish to make -and I think it will be equally effective in disposing of this matter-concerns the rules of this house, in particular standing order 26 paragraph 6(c) which states:
The motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session.
I submit to you, sir, that the burden, the substance of what we have been dealing with today has been dealt with already in the debate which took place in this house on Thursday and Friday.
For these reasons I submit this is not a motion you should rule in order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Halifax should be congratulated on having done his best on behalf of the government side to avoid a discussion of this matter in
U.S. State Department Press Release the terms in which the motion is being put forward. I am afraid, however, he does not find himself, in so far as his main argument is concerned, in harmony with the leader of the house or with the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has considered this statement by the United States government to be of such an unprecedented character that he felt it necessary to bring it up at once in the House of Commons under motions. The Prime Minister himself admits this is a matter of unprecedented urgency, and if that is the case surely we should be permitted-indeed, it is our duty-to discuss a matter of such unprecedented urgency at once in this chamber.
There is one alternative procedure which, if the government saw fit to adopt it, might justify the withdrawal of this motion. If the leader of the house would inform us that at once, when we finish the orders of the day, we would consider the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, which are already before the house, that would also provide a good opportunity to discuss this whole business.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if you should decide, as I hope you will not, on some technical ground that this motion is inadmissible, I hope the government will not run away from the discussion, because they have the opportunity of bringing on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs this afternoon which would provide an ample basis for such a discussion as I am proposing.

subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
To assist you, Mr. Speaker, in reaching a decision as to whether this is urgent I wish to submit that we have had several interpretations of what the defence policy of this country is supposed to be, even since the debate we had on defence policy last week end. Because of this situation I think it is urgent that the members of this house and the country generally should have a clearcut statement of policy from the government. The urgency of the matter involves clearing up this confusion. Delay involves placing the friendship of this country with one of our great neighbours in jeopardy. Therefore I think the urgency of debate is unquestionable.
I should like to say that members of this party do not agree in its entirety with the motion which has been put forward; in other words, that the department of state has contradicted recent statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence. We do not read that out of the release. However, we do feel it urgent that this matter of defence policy should be cleared up.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must surely be clear that if in recent years there has been a subject concerning which there was urgency of debate, this is it.
I thank the hon. member for Halifax for drawing attention to the key sentences, in Beauchesne as far as motions of this kind are concerned. He is perfectly right in saying there must be urgency of debate. I thank him also for reading the sentence which says that the issue must be so pressing that the public interest would suffer if it were not given immediate attention.
Aside from the views expressed by the hon. member for Halifax we find, on the question of urgency, almost unanimous support from the floor of the house. The Prime Minister found it a matter of such urgency, as the Leader of the Opposition noted, that he rose to speak on the matter immediately motions were called. The Leader of the Opposition came into this house with a motion ready under standing order 26. The hon. member for Red Deer tried to move one as well, and my own leader indicated he had one ready. This means that in all four corners of this house it has been recognized that this matter is one of urgency in terms of having a debate today.
I also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is real point to the words quoted by the hon. member for Halifax, which I read a moment ago, that the issue must be so pressing that the public interest would suffer if it is not given immediate attention. I submit that is precisely the case. I submit that unless this statement which was issued at a quarter after six last night by the United States department of state is discussed in this House of Commons, unless we in this House of Commons make our views known, and unless we get a clarification of the position of the government with regard to this whole matter, the Canadian public interest will suffer on all counts. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that although you were acting as you should in inviting comments on this question rather than ruling immediately, the burden of the argument is crystal clear, that this is a matter which comes under the designation of urgency of debate.
One of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Halifax is, I confess, so weak that one should hardly mention it, but he put it forward. He cited the section of standing order 26 which says that one cannot move under that standing order to debate something which has been discussed previously in this session. This house adjourned at six o'clock yesterday. The press release which has given this country such great concern was issued at a quarter after six last


night, so there could not have been any discussion of this matter prior to this occasion. Therefore I suggest that that part of the hon. member's argument should not have been made at all.
Like the hon. member for Medicine Hat I must say that had my leader been able to put forward a motion under standing order 26 there might have been a slightly different turn put on the matter, and if he gets the chance to speak he will so indicate. But what is before us is not any particular implication in the motion of the Leader of the Opposition. What is before us is a request that this house adjourn all its other business to discuss this most urgent and most important matter, the determination of which I suggest should be discussed by this house.

Mr. Speaker, on occasions when you are faced with decisions dealing with motions of this nature you have to take into account a number of factors, the chief one, of course, being urgency of debate. On a great many occasions the subject that is introduced is a matter of very great interest. But then your habit has been to examine the procedure of the house to see whether or not the business set for the day in question should be put aside, as it would have to be put aside to provide for debate if no other opportunity was evident in the near future. Time after time successive Speakers have considered matters of this sort, and if they have been informed or have seen that opportunities for debate would arise in the near future they have not accepted the motion.
In this instance, despite the active interest displayed in this particular matter, there will be opportunities for complete debate on the subject if so desired by the house, and at much greater length than would be the case today, if the general order of business is followed. I announced in the house last night that today and tomorrow we would be discussing estimates; and these are very important estimates, the Department of Labour, Post Office Department, and others. There has been a great demand for discussion of the estimates put forward time and time again by members of the opposition. Now we are being asked to set aside an urgent matter of importance to the Canadian people, namely the spending program of the Canadian government. We are asked to put that aside in favour of entering upon a debate based on a statement made by a foreign country.
In the order of business that I announced yesterday there was a supply motion for Monday and Tuesday. That provides a two day debate on a subject selected by the opposition and leads to a conclusion, because votes are called at the end of supply motions. The debate today would not be a conclusive debate, because it would end when the automatic adjournment of the house occurs.

The question that concerns me is whether there will be an opportunity to discuss this important matter, such that we do not need to interrupt the proceedings to deal with it today, or whether there has already been ample opportunity this-session.
It seems to me this is one of the essential considerations which Your Honour will wish to bear in mind. From the nod of Your Honour's head, I gather that you concur in this observation. The fact that this is a matter of urgency is, in my opinion, reflected in the very character of the circumstances which brought the Prime Minister to his feet when Your Honour called motions. In his own words is to be found the justification for our plea of urgency. The Prime Minister said in substance that never before in the relations between the two countries had there been so unwarranted an intervention by the United States in the affairs of this country. That statement in itself, in the light of the-situation that confronts us in the world, surely should constitute evidence of the-urgency of the matter. Do we need any further evidence? In the statement of the Prime Minister we have evidence that so urgent is this matter, that the government has given instructions to our ambassador in Washington to return to Canada at once for consultation with the government at home. Can there be anything which reflects more seriously than does that action the urgency of this situation?
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if you were to determine that there was no urgency-

I wish to thank all hon.
members who have assisted me at arriving at a decision in this regard. The motion of the Leader of the Opposition refers to a statement which was released yesterday contradicting certain statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence concerning certain joint defence arrangements of the Canadian and the United States governments.
I think everyone agrees that this matter is one of great importance. Hence the question to be decided is whether or not we should

spend some time in discussing such a matter. The question that concerns me is that of urgency of debate at this time.
As I have indicated, and as have my predecessors on many occasions, rule 26 is a very extraordinary remedy. There are ample references to it on precisely the key point, namely the urgency of debate. If, as seemed to be indicated by certain hon. members, the question was that of the acquisition of nuclear weapons, then I would immediately say no, as that matter was debated last week. So on that ground the proposition, as it affects the country as a whole, would fall to the ground.
As to the question of urgency of debate by reason of the fact that this was the first item on motions, we have motions called five days a week, and I fail to see how in many instances there can be differences as to the timing or as to what person puts forward a matter when the Speaker calls motions.
There is another point urged with regard to urgency of debate, and that is the necessity of ascertaining the facts. On the basis that this statement was issued at 6.15 p.m. yesterday, and as hon. members are here, I find some difficulty in seeing how a general debate in this connection could ascertain more facts than have been disclosed at the present time. In combination with something else I feel that if the purpose is to ascertain the facts today, this is not necessarily the most appropriate time.
It has been indicated by the hon. member for Essex East in citing a ruling of my predecessor that there should have been a recent opportunity in the past to discuss the matter, and I agree with him that in so far as the narrow confines of this statement are concerned there was not that opportunity. But there will certainly be an opportunity in the relatively near future. This is not a new indication this afternoon but something that was indicated yesterday and even the day before. It has been announced that the business for next Monday will be a supply motion. This provides for a two day debate if required and also provides for some form of conclusion if such shall be the case, whereas the adjournment of the business today would merely result in the discussion of this matter without any conclusion.
Notwithstanding the fact that there is a great deal of interest in these matters, I still find on these grounds that such a motion does not meet the requirements in so far as urgency of debate is concerned. Therefore I would not accept the motion.

Subsequently, on March 27 and on May 22, 1935, under Mr. Speaker Bowman, appeals were allowed without even going to this second stage.
Mr. Speaker, I have browsed enough in the procedures and practices of parliament to know that there are incidents since then when rulings have been given the other way. I suggest the rulings have been back and forth to such an extent that there is no clear decision by the parliament of Canada on this point. If the Minister of Public Works is going to rely on the stand taken by Mr. Speaker Black on February 19, 1932, I suggest he should look and see what Mr. Speaker Black did on November 2, 1932, some months later in the same year, when he allowed an appeal.
This is a new parliament, and we have our own problems to deal with. There is no clear precedent. There are precedents both ways. I submit that in effect you have ruled today-you, Mr. Speaker Lambert, have ruled -that there is no appeal against your ruling. It is your ruling that must be tested. Irrespective of the provocation-and there was provocation-it was wrong of the state department of the United States or the foreign office of any government, however friendly, to issue a statement of this kind commenting on-and by commenting on in this way, intervening in-a matter which is before the House of Commons of this country. speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not been in Washington for many months.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There have been a good many visits to Washington, since my last visit, by members of the government, who must know much more about these matters than I do. The Prime Minister went to Nassau a little while ago where he had luncheon with the President of the United States. No doubt he talked with the President of the United States about these matters on that occasion. May I ask him whether he discussed with the President of the United States the propriety of bringing these matters into the House of Commons and giving the United States government notice that he was going to do so? I am sure that in this luncheon conversation between the President of the United States and the Prime Minister they went over the whole question of Canadian-American relations.
With respect to these negotiations about which we heard for the first time last Friday, having been told two years ago by the Prime Minister that discussions on this matter had ceased, there is a paragraph in the United States communique which should be put on the record because it bears on the origin of these conversations, these discussions, these negotiations, which were first made public by the Prime Minister of this country without any consultation with the government of the United States. I read from the United States communique:
Shortly after the Cuban crisis in October 1962-
Shortly after the Cuban crisis.
-the Canadian government proposed confidential discussions-
The initiative for these confidential discussions came not from the United States but from the Canadian government. The proposal was made by the Canadian government for such conversations, for such discussions. Surely that makes it all the more important that if disclosure of these confidential negotiations was to be made by the Prime Minister in a debate in the House of Commons it would have been done with the knowledge and approval of the other party to the negotiations. I know the Prime Minister is a stickler for the proprieties in these matters.


I know how he feels when he does not get more than half an hour's notice. How does he think the United States government felt when it got no notice at all?
Shortly after the Cuban crisis In October 1962, the Canadian government proposed confidential discussions concerning circumstances under which there might be provision of nuclear weapons for Canadian armed forces in Canada and Europe.
This was the proposal made by the Canadian government for conversations with the United States government. The communique goes on:
These discussions have been exploratory in nature; the Canadian government has not as yet proposed any arrangement sufficiently practical to contribute effectively to North American defence.
So much for the negotiations about which we have been unable up to the present to secure any information in this house, although the Prime Minister himself in the debate last Friday, and the Minister of National Defence, did tell us they were going on. Perhaps we will hear this evening from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) at least what department of the Canadian government is carrying on these confidential negotiations, what progress is being made, if any, and why it is that the Canadian government, having proposed them for the purpose set out in this paragraph, has not been able to put forward any practical suggestion which might contribute effectively to the joint defence? The communique also has this to say:
In 1958 the Canadian government decided to adopt the Bomarc-B weapons systems. Accordingly two Bomarc-B squadrons were deployed to Canada-
At the expense, incidentally, of the United States government.
-where they would serve the double purpose of protecting Montreal and Toronto as well as the U.S. deterrent force. The Bomarc-B was not designed to carry any conventional warhead.
Of course, we all knew that.
The matter of making available a nuclear warhead for it and for other nuclear capable weapons systems acquired by Canada has been the subject of inconclusive discussions between the two governments. The installation of the two Bomarc-B batteries in Canada without nuclear warheads was completed in 1962.
That confirms what we on this side felt to be the case, that by the end of 1962 the point of no return had been reached in so far as these two Bomarc squadrons were concerned in regard to keeping them there without any warheads or giving them the warheads without which they would be completely useless. Then the communique goes on:
In addition to the Bomarc-B, a similar problem exists with respect to the modern supersonic jet interceptor-

I believe that is the CF-101.
-with which the R.C.A.F. has been provided. Without nuclear air defence warheads, they operate at far less than their full potential effectiveness.
One of the statements made by the Prime Minister in the debate last Friday which must have caused some confusion in the mind of the Minister of National Defence and, indeed, of the other party to our defence arrangements, the United States government, was a statement made by the Prime Minister who has stated more than once in the discussions we have had on this matter in the house that there is no contradiction between anything he said last Friday and the clarifying statement issued by the Minister of National Defence. No contradiction, the Prime Minister has told us. But the Prime Minister said last Friday, as found on page 3133 of Hansard, that these aircraft, the CF-101 that is referred to in the paragraph in the communique which I read, "title to which will be vested in Canada, will be armed with conventional weapons".
But if you look at the statement by the Minister of National Defence, which no doubt he will clarify further in the course of this discussion, you will find that he says:
So far as NORAD is concerned, Canada has been negotiating with the United States for the past two to three months in order that nuclear warheads will be made available for our two squadrons of Bomarcs and our F-101 interceptors.
That is only one contradiction between the policy as laid down by the Prime Minister and the policy on defence as clarified by the Minister of National Defence, so perhaps in addition to dealing with the statement from Washington the two hon. gentlemen concerned will reconcile their own clarifications, with assistance from the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny). Then the communique goes on to say:
The discussions between the two governments have also involved possible arrangements for the provision of nuclear weapons for Canadian NATO forces in Europe-
That is a straightforward statement.
The discussions between the two governments have also involved possible arrangements for the provision of nuclear weapons for Canadian NATO forces in Europe, similar to the arrangements which the United States has made with many of our NATO allies.
We will expect the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence or both to clarify that statement in the light of its relation to statements made by the Prime Minister in the house last Friday. I continue with the communique:
During the debate in the House of Commons various references were made to recent discussions
at Nassau.
U.S. State Department Press Release
Now, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a great play on the fact that the conference at Nassau between the United States president and the United Kingdom prime minister had a very direct and definite bearing on Canadian defence policy in NATO and perhaps even, so far as I know, in NORAD.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: And all the nations of NATO.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: U.S. STATE DEPARTMENT PRESS RELEASE   MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
If that happens to be the case, and of course it is not the situation, why is it that the Prime Minister then would make a statement of that kind, which would certainly be a great surprise to the other members of NATO who were not at the conference, and which is not borne out by anything in the Nassau communique from the United Kingdom and the United States. Either the Prime Minister had some secret information which he is disclosing to this house and which the other NATO governments know nothing about, or he is basing his statement on a communique that does not support it.
After all, the United States was a party to this conference and presumably the United States government knows more about the implications of the Nassau agreement between President Kennedy and Prime Minister Macmillan than the Prime Minister of Canada could hope to know, because he did not take part in these discussions. He had lunch with the two leaders but, regrettably, he did not take part in the discussions. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this paragraph on Nassau has very special significance. It reads:
During the debate in the House of Commons various references were made to recent discussions at Nassau. The agreements made at Nassau have been fully published.
Apparently there are no secret agreements; they have been fully published.
They raise no question of the appropriateness of nuclear weapons for Canadian forces in fulfilling their NATO or NORAD obligations.
The Prime Minister told us that this statement made by one party to these discussions at Nassau is inaccurate. Does he continue to insist on the validity of his own argument that the Nassau communique and the Nassau conversations did have that effect which the United States government says in its communique they did not have?
Then, Mr. Speaker, the second last paragraph of this United States communique reads:
Reference was also made in the debate to the need of NATO for increased conventional forces. A flexible and balanced defence requires increased conventional forces,-
We on this side have said this more than once both in and out of the house.
3304	HOUSE OF
U.S. State Department Press Release -but conventional forces are not an alternative to effective NATO or NORAD defence arrangements using nuclear-capable weapons systems.
Perhaps the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) or both hon. gentlemen could comment on the authority for that particular statement. The United States statement continues:
NORAD is designed to defend the North American continent against air attack. The Soviet bomber fleet will remain at least throughout this decade a significant element in the Soviet strike force. An effective continental defence against this common threat is necessary.
Then, the last paragraph reads:
The provision of nuclear weapons to Canadian forces would not involve an expansion of independent nuclear capability, or an increase in the "nuclear club". As in the case of other allies custody of U.S. nuclear weapons would remain with the U.S. joint control fully consistent with national sovereignty can be worked out to cover the use of such weapons by Canadian forces.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this communique is extremely interesting, regardless of the impropriety of issuing it at all, and I claim it was improper to issue it. This is extremely interesting because of the light it throws on the confusions and contradictions of Canadian defence policy. Anyone who has listened to the Prime Minister's statement, to the Minister of National Defence's clarification, to the Secretary of State for External Affairs' (Mr. Green) statements, can understand how confusion can be caused in these matters by these contradictory statements.
May I just refer to one such contradiction? In the statement made by the Prime Minister last Friday, as recorded on page 3127 of Hansard.
-we will act to do those things that will carry out our responsibilities.
I think no one will take any exception to that statement. Then he went on to say, in respect of responsibilities.
We will do nothing to extend the nuclear family.
But having made that statement, on page 3128, the following page, he added this:
-those forces-
He was talking about some of the Canadian forces with NORAD and NATO.
-would have to be equipped, in order to be fully effective, with defensive nuclear weapons if and when the need arose.
The Prime Minister will do nothing to extend the nuclear family but he has accepted, on behalf of the government of Canada, equipment which cannot be effective without nuclear warheads and he is willing to accept those nuclear warheads if and when the need arises.
The Minister of National Defence is a little more specific on this matter. I refer to 

his statement, no doubt in clarification of the Prime Minister's statement that we will do nothing to extend the nuclear family, when he said:
-our obligations to equip certain weapons systems with nuclear arms are reiterated together with the determination to honour those obligations.
Take your pick, Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the Minister of National Defence or the remarks of the Prime Minister of Canada. How both of these hon. gentlemen can reconcile these contradictory remarks and maintain there is cabinet solidarity is difficult for anyone on this side of the house to understand. The Minister of National Defence brings it all to a conclusion in his clarifying statement when he says this:
Those paragraphs-
He is referring to certain paragraphs in the Prime Minister's speech.
-state a definite policy for the acquisition of nuclear arms.
Well, Mr. Speaker, surely I have said enough to underline the contradictions, the confusions that have been created by the Prime Minister, not by the United States government, in his statement of last Friday. Surely, I have said enough to indicate that if it was improper for the United States to issue this release, as it was, it was equally improper for the Prime Minister of this country to make public the fact that there were negotiations going on between the United States and this government without getting the approval of the other party to the negotiations, and without even informing them of the disclosure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate and the arguments which have been developed in it turn in two directions. One is really not germane to the debate at all and yet there has been a good deal of discussion on it. I refer to the question as to whether these surcharges are in fact legal. I shall later deal with that matter at some length, even though it may appear to be out of order. I shall do so for this reason, that much of the time of the house has been taken up in discussing that very point. I suggest it is really because of the lack of understanding of the point and why it is irrelevant to this debate that hon. members in certain parts of the house have in the past indicated that they would support this motion.
In order that we may deal with this situation comprehensively I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members that the

Correspondence Respecting Surcharge argument for having these documents produced, based on precedent, was completely demolished by my friend the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith). He completely demolished the arguments of the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). He made a very interesting analysis of the arguments that had been put forward up to that time, and the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Simcoe North have shown completely that there is no precedent worthy of consideration that supports this motion. I should like to refer hon. members to Hansard of November 22, starting at page 1912 and continuing through the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe North, who made a brilliant speech. Perhaps the ability with which he presented his arguments and the validity of those arguments can be demonstrated by the fact that he was interrupted on no less than 17 occasions by members of the opposition and that on no less than seven occasions Your Honour had to restore order and intervene in the debate, in order to allow the hon. member to continue his remarks.
The arguments of the hon. member for Essex East which were demolished by those put forward by the hon. member for Simcoe North commence at the beginning of the second column of page 1912. He quotes them chapter and verse. I shall quote them in summary so that hon. members may understand that there is no substance at all in the arguments and there is no precedent for the production of these documents. The precedents cited originally by the hon. member for Essex East are as follows. He first referred to an opinion given by the minister of justice in 1935, which is referred to at page 1427 of the current Hansard. As reported on that page, the hon. member for Essex East said:
Not only did he give without any prodding the opinion of the law officers of the crown but as well he volunteered opinions on the very point in issue which had been tendered by two eminent counsel, namely Mr. W. N. Tilley, K.C. and Mr. Aime Geoffrion, on the very point. Those opinions are now to be found in Hansard for 1935, volume III, at page 3166.
That is the end of the quotation from the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East. Then we have the observations and comment of the hon. member for Simcoe North clearly destroying that argument. He said, as reported at page 1912 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the opinion of the law officers of the crown on that occasion was not given.
That is the answer to that argument. Then he said:
There was no request for it. All that was done was that Mr. Guthrie, as reported at page 3166 of volume III of Hansard for 1935 said:

"The opinion of the law officers of the crown is that clause 5 presents some difficulties."
Then a little further on he said:
"The opinions of counsel who 1 have named are summed up in the following statement by Mr. Tilley:"
The hon. member for Essex East had read Mr. Tilley's opinion, he being an independent counsel. This question was pursued in the house on that occasion by the hon. member for Simcoe North, who said:
On that occasion, notwithstanding what was said by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Essex East, the opinion of the law officers of the crown was not produced.
It was the same dispute. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) said it was given in the house. My hon. friend from Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) said it was not. The reply given was: "You have just read it." To this the answer, naturally, was that only the substance had been given. That completely disposes of the argument of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).
The second precedent the hon. member quoted appears at page 1427 of Hansard for 1962 as follows:
...we have as perhaps the most recent precedent In this house the action taken by Mr. St. Laurent when he was minister of justice. In May of 1942 the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Cardiff) and the present member for that constituency moved for a copy of all opinions rendered by the Department of Justice with reference to the power of the governor in council to conscript men for service in any theatre of war.
Subsequently Mr. St. Laurent tabled those opinions. The hon. member for Simcoe North effectively disposed of that argument when he referred hon. members to a motion which is to be found on page 2290 of Hansard for 1942. The motion is as follows:
For a copy of all opinions rendered by the Department of Justice with reference to the power of the governor in council under the War Measures Act to conscript men for service in any theatre of war.
Mr. Cardiff had asked for a copy of all opinions rendered by the Department of Justice with respect to this matter, and Mr. St. Laurent replied:
I have been advised by the departments of government concerned to say that they do not object to the production of the opinions mentioned in this motion, but it will be done without prejudice to the general rule-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks this afternoon I was asking the Canadian government to take advantage of this motion to discuss Canadian defence policy, and in doing so to examine, if it so desires, the United States government statement which, I repeat, should not have been issued in the first place but which, having been issued, is a further link in the chain of evidence which exposes the confusions, the contradictions, the weakness and the indecision of Canadian defence policy today as part of continental, and indeed collective, defence policy. The reason we on this side of the house believe that such a discussion is a matter of urgent importance, and the reason we are joined in this opinion by two of the three other parties in this house, has nothing to do with United States opinions about Canadian policies which may be implied in that statement. As I have said, such an expression of opinion in these circumstances was unwarranted and unjustified. I know that the United States government had plenty of provocation. It had before it the spectacle of the government which had joined with it in continental defence, the government which had made in July, 1957 the NORAD agreement with it, apparently publicly divided about matters which were of course of close concern to the United States, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) saying one thing and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) saying something else, with the Minister of National Defence apparently engaged in negotiations with the United States to carry out his policy, and the Prime Minister disclosing these confidential negotiations last Friday but certainly not explaining them.
However, Mr. Speaker, whatever the provocation, two wrongs do not make a right and to the extent that it expressed or implied opinions, the United States government was wrong in making this public statement. But the primary interest of this house is not in


the opinions of the United States government. Our interest lies in finding out the facts for and about Canada, the facts as to what is the present defence policy of this Canadian government. The Prime Minister has told one story, the Minister of National Defence has told another; the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) sit silent. It is left to our neighbour and ally to tell yet another story, one much closer to that of the Minister of National Defence than to the Prime Minister's, but different in important respects from both. We want the facts, Mr. Speaker, all the facts, about the defence policy of Canada.
The Canadian people have the right to know. If our allies want to know too, as they apparently do, that is natural in a coalition, but it is secondary. It is of first importance however that the Canadian people know. Any government that evades any longer telling them, that evades saying what are its own policies in this vital matter, is guilty of neglect of its duty to the Canadian people.
This motion, which the government opposed, does give the government another chance to tell us now. However, Mr. Speaker, it will not be helpful, to say the least-and it could be harmful-if, instead of doing this, government spokesmen retreat into cheap slanders about the motives of those of us on this side in the statements that we make on defence. So far as my own motives are concerned, I will let the record speak about my service to my country, and of my pride in that service over the many years as a Canadian, but as one who knows that service to Canada cannot be divorced from service to peace and to freedom. These irritating but idle slanders, Mr. Speaker, are merely a smokescreen for those who wish to obscure their own defaults and take people's minds ofE the serious problems which we face in this country today and which we must solve. It would be a sorry day for us all if we allowed-or, even worse, if we encouraged-differences and disputes between our two countries to weaken, and perhaps even destroy, the good neighbourhood which we have built up over the years and which of course has had to stand, and will have to stand, many strains. It is now more essential than ever that both countries, as partners in a coalition of other free and democratic nations for peace and progress, preserve and strengthen that good neighbourhood inside the coalition in which the United States alone have the power to give the leadership that is required-I pray that it also has the wisdom-in that coalition in which Canada has played and, I hope, will continue to play, a good and responsible part. I do not propose, and we on this side do not

propose, to do anything which would blur or weaken that part. Whenever the western alliance is weakened and divided, only Moscow and Peking are happy; and there are sombre signs of such a division in Europe today. I hope they will disappear. In any event, let us not carry this division across the Atlantic or do anything which would injure good relations on this continent. At least, let us make sure that if this is done we do not have any responsibility on our side of the border for that deterioration.
It was said this afternoon that Canada and Canadians are not going to be pushed around by anyone. Of course we are not. Canada will manage its own affairs. But we cannot do this in isolation from our friends or by quarrelling needlessly with them. Canada first, yes: The right kind of nationalism is a healthy and strong thing in the building of a country. Canada first, yes: But to say "Canada only" would be wrong and impossible. Let us be mature enough to accept both these guides for conduct in our relations with the United States of America and with our other friends. If our two countries sharing this continent, so close together in so many ways, cannot maintain a solid structure of friendship and close co-operation founded on respect for each other's national identity and national independence, then ideed there is little hope for peace, security and progress in the troubled world of today. I say this: in defence and in everything else we can stand up for Canada, as we will; we can protect our rights and safeguard our interests, as we will. But I insist on believing we can do this while maintaining close and good relations with our neighbours. As Canadians-and all members of the house are Canadians and proud to be Canadians-we on this side will do our best to avoid any such disastrous results coming from any temporary differences which may exist between our two countries and which, I do believe, by good sense, moderation and understanding on both sides, can easily be solved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has been precipitated by a press release which was issued by the United States state department yesterday. All parties in this house have gone on record as regretting and resenting this interference in what is a matter of public debate in the House of Commons and something which should be settled by the people of Canada alone. However, Mr. Speaker, we ought not to allow any feeling of resentment to cause us to lose our sense of perspective with regard to this matter. I think we have a right to tell the Americans that we will decide this matter for ourselves. But even this course need not interfere with the good relations between Canada and the United States. We have strong bonds of blood, language and trade as well as common ideals of justice, democracy and liberty which will always bind us closely together.
The Leader of the Opposition made a great play with regard to the importance of friendship between these two neighbouring countries. With that sentiment all of us will agree. However, I submit that independence of thought and expression need not mean division. In the communist bloc where a group of satellites are held in thrall by the Soviet union, obedience is the watchword. However, in the west we have always prided ourselves

on the fact that what we have is a free association of free people and that where there is a free association of free people we should have the right to express our differences of opinion. This ought not to diminish our friendship. As a matter of fact, it is sometimes easier to tell your neighbour and your friend to mind his own business than it is to tell a stranger to do so. That is all we have tried to do today, without in any way meaning that we are seeking to divide these two nations in the many things which they have in common.
Independence in matters of international affairs is something for which the Canadian people have struggled over the years. There was in our history a time when we were still tied to London by strings of colonialism. Men like Sir Robert Borden in the first world war and Right Hon. Mackenzie King at the beginning of the second world war insisted that Canada had a right to make its own decisions and that we did not take instructions from Whitehall. In the second half of the twentieth century it is equally important that, without being offensive, we can say that we are not prepared to take instructions either from the pentagon or Whitehall.
What I resent most about the statement which was issued yesterday by the state department of the United States is not just that it criticized the head of a government of a friendly country but that it sought to put pressure on the Canadian people to adopt a policy with which I disagree. But irrespective of whether I disagree with it or not, it is a policy which the Canadian people have the right to adopt or reject on their own, without interference by others.
The second thing I think we should keep in mind is that this statement which was issued yesterday simply points up the fact that the Canadian government has not been straightforward and honest in acquainting the Canadian people regarding its intentions concerning the acquisition of nuclear arms. This afternoon the Prime Minister said that this statement from Washington would in no way change the government's statement. As I said this afternoon, which statement? We have had two policies enunciated by the government and all this furore has been because we are trying to get the government to come down on one side or the other so that the Canadian people will know what our policy is in respect of the acquisition of nuclear arms.
Over the years this government has accepted commitments to acquire equipment and planes which were virtually useless unless they were equipped with nuclear warheads. Yet the government has continued to give the impression that even though they

were buying this equipment no irrevocable decision had been made to acquire these nuclear warheads. Always the suggestion has been thrown out that "some time in the future we will be able to make this decision". What we have really been doing is to spend hundreds of millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money buying equipment which is worthless if we do not accept nuclear warheads, and which puts us into the nuclear club if we do.
The Prime Minister himself put on the record last Friday his well known statement at Brockville during the election campaign where he said:
We shall not, so long as we are pursuing the ways of disarmament, allow the extension of the nuclear family into Canada . . . We do not intend to allow the spread of nuclear arms beyond the nations which now have them.
That seems a very clearcut statement. Now we find as a result of the statement that was made first by the Prime Minister and then by the Minister of National Defence, and now by the state department, that negotiations are going on at the present time to acquire nuclear arms even though the prospects for disarmament are much brighter now than they have been for some time.
Let me point out some of the inconsistencies. In his statement last Friday the Prime Minister, as found on page 3128 of Hansard, said:
In 1958, when the Bomarc was first laid down as a plan, the great challenge to North America was believed to be bombers carrying bombs ... Today that is changed. More and more there is a phasing out in connection with the bomber threat as more and more intercontinental ballistic missiles are increasing in number.
That statement by the Prime Minister is supported by the statement which appeared in today's press containing an announcement made by Mr. McNamara, secretary of state for defence in Washington yesterday. Mr. McNamara said:
Bomarc anti aircraft missiles, which cost the United States about ?2 billion, have only a limited life. These weapons suffer from the same defects as manned interceptors, vulnerability to ballistic missile attack. But because the United States already has paid for its eight Bomarc sites, the Bomarc system will be continued for several years. Canada has two Bomarc squadrons, but no nuclear warheads for them.
In the same statement Mr. McNamara said:
The main continental concentration must be in defence against the expanding intercontinental missile threat. The United States is moving ahead with research on a more advanced form of antimissile defence known as the Nike-X, but there will be no production until the system is able to discriminate between a real nuclear missile and a decoy.
If it is true that the Bomarc has a very short life, a very limited effectiveness, and
TJ.S. State Department Press Release that manned bombers are no longer a real threat, then it seems to me the government ought to tell us why it is that they now propose, according to the Minister of National Defence, to negotiate agreements to accept nuclear warheads for them. In the same speech of last Friday the Prime Minister made this significant statement:
More and more the nuclear deterrent is becoming of such a nature that more nuclear arms will add nothing materially to our defences. Greater and greater emphasis must be placed on conventional arms and conventional forces.
I ask the house to consider that statement in the light of the statements which were made by the Minister of National Defence and by the state department. As found on page 3136 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
Delivery of the F-104G has commenced, but the strike reconnaissance role has been placed under doubt by the recent Nassau declaration concerning nuclear arms...
He went on to say:
It will be necessary, therefore, at this meeting in May, for Canada to give consideration to this matter and we will, in co-operation with the nations of NATO, undertake a clarification of our role in NATO defence plans and disposition.
In the light of these statements let us look now at what the Minister of National Defence said. I must say in passing that to the best of my knowledge this is the first time that 72 hours after a prime minister has made an important statement on policy in parliament one of his ministers has found it necessary to issue a statement of clarification and interpretation and to make it outside of the house where he could not be questioned or interrogated on the matter. The Minister of National Defence, referring to page 3136 of Hansard for January 25, sums up the Prime Minister's statement by saying:
Those paragraphs state a definite policy for the acquisition of nuclear arms in these terms.
That certainly is not the impression that those of us who listened to the speech or those of us who read it carefully clause by clause next day got from it. The Minister of National Defence then sums up the three paragraphs and says:
First, our obligations to equip certain weapons systems with nuclear arms are reiterated, together with the determination to honour those obligations.
What obligations? This is what we want to know; what are the obligations? If the Canadian government decides to commit Canada into the nuclear club, then the Canadian people ought to know it. They ought to know what obligations have been assumed. If the minister says we are going to honour those obligations, then this parliament and the people of this country ought to know what it is we are going to honour, and what it is we

U.S. State Department Press Release are going to do. The minister who says we are going to honour these obligations has not yet spoken in parliament, although we have been sitting tor months, to tell us what our obligations are.
Second, that the strike reconnaissance role of the F-104's has been placed in some doubt by the recent Nassau declaration, as well as other developments in the defence field; thus, it is necessary for Canada to seek, on the part of NATO, a clarification of her role in NATO defence plans and dispositions; this clarification to be provided when the NATO ministerial meeting is held in Canada next May. Should NATO reaffirm for Canada a role involving nuclear weapons, Canada will equip her NATO forces to discharge her obligation.
Surely, that is crystal clear, beyond any shadow of doubt. It is not this parliament, it is not this government; it is our NATO allies who will decide whether or not to reaffirm Canada's role involving nuclear weapons. Now, it is bad enough when any one country, even a friendly neighbour, is going to lay down our policy; but is the NATO council now going to lay down our policy? This is certainly the implication in this statement. Of course, as the release from the state department points out, this whole question of the Nassau declaration placing this matter in doubt is a sheer hallucination and is simply another means of postponing making a decision, a decision which this government has been putting off month after month and year after year.
I say it is time for them to take their courage in their hands. Sooner or later, they have to come down on the side of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) who has been against nuclear weapons, or the defence minister who has been for nuclear weapons. Any government, any individual who tries to ride two horses going in opposite directions is bound to find himself sitting in a most undignified position. This is exactly the plight into which the government has brought itself at the present time.
I continue with the minister's statement:
Third, so far as NORAD is concerned, Canada has been negotiating with the United States for the past two to three months in order that nuclear warheads will be made available for our two squadrons of Bomarcs and for the F-101 interceptor squadrons. These negotiations will be continued in order to reach a satisfactory agreement. I believe such an agreement can be arrived at in the near future.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that in both the statement of the Prime Minister and the defence minister, only NORAD is mentioned as being the subject of nuclear negotiations with the United States. However, the state department release yesterday says that there have been confidential discussions proposed by the Canadian government concerning circumstances under which there might
[Mr. Douglas.!

be provision of nuclear weapons for Canadian armed forces in Canada and Europe. We were not, therefore, told all the story. I might point out also that the minister's statement refers to nuclear warheads for the F-101 interceptor planes, but the Prime Minister's statement says that these would be armed with conventional weapons.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to labour the point. I feel it is quite clear that the government has been unable to make up its mind. Since 1958 it has been playing both sides of the street. Now, events have caught up with them. The Prime Minister said last Friday that the government's policy was flexible and fluid. It has not been either flexible or fluid, it has become wiley and wobbly; it has wobbled from one side to the other. Theirs has been a program of postponement and procrastination. I hope the government will make up its mind. I hope it will make up its mind in favour of a nonnuclear role for Canada. But what I fear is that we are, behind closed doors, being committed inch by inch to nuclear weapons, so that suddenly we will wake up to find ourselves members of the world's nuclear club.
The statement by the minister of defence, and the statement by the state department yesterday, make it fairly clear to me at least that the policy of the government on nuclear weapons is not substantially different from that of the Liberal party, except that the Liberal party has come out forthrightly now and said that they are in favour of accepting nuclear weapons for Canada. The government seems to be edging into it backwards, bit by bit, by secret negotiations and the buying of equipment which is worthless without nuclear warheads. The end result, of course, will be the same. The Liberal party wants to go into the nuclear club through the front door and then, if they can, negotiate themselves out the back door. The government, apparently, wants to sneak in under cover of darkness through the back door so nobody will see them going in.
We in this party have made our position abundantly clear. We say that Canada should negotiate itself out of any nuclear commitments under both NORAD and NATO. I do not need to reiterate the arguments. The Prime Minister himself gave some of them last Friday when he said that nuclear arms would not add materially to our safety, that the real threat in the future is from intercontinental ballistic missiles, that our contribution could be made by the use of conventional arms or conventional forces. They are all there. The official opposition, the Liberal party, really do not want a nuclear role for Canada either, because they say that even if they get nuclear weapons, the moment

they get them and train people to use them, they are going to try to get rid of them. Then why not start by not accepting them in the first place.
We think this is the time to speak out independently, as other nations in NATO have done, Norway, Denmark and others. We say there is nothing to be gained by joining the nuclear club, but there is much to be lost; that the whole trend today in military strategy is away from the limited nuclear, tactical war; that the two great powers now have the ultimate nuclear deterrent; that as long as it is restricted to these two powers, the horrible consequences of a nuclear war may deter them both, and that therefore Canada's best contribution lies in containment, in preventing nuclear weapons from spreading to nations other than the two which now have them. We say that this is the first step as a prelude to getting a ban on nuclear tests and ultimately an international treaty for nuclear disarmament under international inspection and control.
We are not suggesting that Canada should wash its hands of its responsibilities. We are a member of the west. We have great responsibilities in this world. But we maintain that those responsibilities, in view of our size, our location and our resources, can best be discharged by giving increasing support to the United Nations, by supplying conventional forces for a world police force, by making available some of our vast resources of food, capital goods and consumer goods to help the underprivileged and needy countries in the world.
May I close by saying this one word, Mr. Speaker. Around the corridors there are constant rumours of a dissolution of this parliament so that this matter can be settled by the people of Canada. I for one believe that if this government or any government, having in mind that all the parties in the last election were against acquiring nuclear weapons for Canada, is going to acquire nuclear weapons, it has a responsibility to go honestly to the people of Canada for a mandate before accepting nuclear weapons which involve the lives, the welfare and the future of the people of this country. I want to say that as far as we in this party are concerned, no talk of a dissolution will intimidate us from trying to find out what our obligations are and from seeking to discover the extent to which this government has committed us to the acquisition of nuclear arms. After all, arguments about United States intervention and arguments about whether or not the government's policy is a made in Canada policy rather than a made in the United States policy are pure
U.S. State Department Press Release irrelevancies. They constitute a smokescreen, a smokescreen that is laced with double talk.
There is only one question at issue in this debate. That question is, to what extent, if any, has the government of Canada committed itself to the acquisition of nuclear arms for its forces? That is what we want to know. We have had contradictory and conflicting statements. We would be derelict in our duty, Mr. Speaker, if we did not insist that the government tell us. It is not a matter of mere academic debate or political manoeuvring. Joining the nuclear club is something which can affect the lives of all the people in this country, of generations yet unborn, and the peace of the world. We have a right to know what is the government's policy. We have a right to know what commitments they have made. We have a right, above all, to have the government come down on one side or the other. We in this party plead with them to come down on the side of giving Canada a conventional and economic aid role in the world, and to stand up before the world and say that in order to promote peace, in order to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, Canada will not become a member of the nuclear club and will not accept nuclear arms.

The Minister of National Defence talked about unity in the cabinet. They all speak the same language. He asserts there is no difficulty with regard to the positions of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and himself. He says nothing, of course, about the views of the Associate Minister of National Defence. We know what the views of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are. He said in a speech in Vancouver on December 4:
There has been no change In policy-that is to decline nuclear weapons until there is a deteriorating world situation or war.
On January 25 the Prime Minister said in this house:
More nuclear arms will add nothing materially to our defences.
That is the statement of the Prime Minister. Then, on the 28th of January in the release,

in the statement of interpretation-the minister does not like the word "clarification"- the Minister of National Defence said that the government is committed to a definite policy for the acquisition of nuclear arms. These excerpts, and I am going to come to more extended ones, clearly indicate that the challenge of the Minister of National Defence is answered, because there is and there continues to be in the very statement he made tonight a clear division of opinion between himself and the statements the Prime Minister made in this house last Friday.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the fact that the Minister of National Defence issued a press release, resorting to that extraordinary action, indicates in itself a serious division of opinion between the Prime Minister and himself as Minister of National Defence. Otherwise, why issue a statement.
